title: Rocío Calderón Madrid
text:
I am Rocío Calderón, a postdoctoral researcher within the MOMENTUM programme at the Institute for Sustainable Agriculture (IAS-CSIC) in Córdoba, Spain. I hold degrees in Agricultural and Civil Engineering and a PhD in Biosciences and Agrifood Sciences from the University of Córdoba. I am currently pursuing a MSc in Biostatistics at the University of Valencia. Throughout my research career, I have worked at several institutions across Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States.
My research focuses on the early detection, surveillance and risk assessment of plant pathogens, including Verticillium dahliae, Xylella fastidiosa and Fusarium oxysporum, through the integration of remote sensing and epidemiological modelling. My current work aims to develop operational surveillance systems for emerging diseases in crops under climate change. To this end, I adopt an integrated digital approach combining satellite and high-resolution airborne hyperspectral and thermal remote sensing, advanced statistical methods for epidemiological modelling, and artificial intelligence. This approach seeks to optimise surveillance and management strategies, reduce the economic and environmental impacts of plant diseases, and safeguard food security, while strengthening the resilience of agricultural ecosystems to climate change and emerging pathogens.

title: Rocío Calderón Madrid
text:
Research interests

Remote sensing of plant health and disease: hyperspectral, multispectral and thermal imaging from airborne and satellite platforms.
Digital surveillance and early-warning systems: integration of remote sensing, statistical modelling and artificial intelligence for emerging plant disease monitoring.
Quantitative plant disease epidemiology: disease dynamics, transmission and spatial spread modelling.
Species distribution and ecological niche modelling: mapping pathogen distributions, identifying environmental drivers and assessing potential range shifts under climate change.
Advanced biostatistical modelling: Bayesian inference, spatial and spatiotemporal models, and statistical approaches for spectral and epidemiological data.
Radiative transfer modelling and vegetation trait retrieval: estimation of biochemical, biophysical and physiological plant traits.
Machine learning, deep learning and data-driven approaches: crop health assessment, disease detection and predictive modelling.

title: MOMENTUM: Remote sensing and epidemiological modelling for the surveillance of emerging plant diseases
text:
About MOMENTUM
MOMENTUM is the CSIC Programme for Attracting and Retaining Digital Talent. It offers four-year contracts that combine an R&D project with a personalised training plan in advanced digital skills, such as artificial intelligence, data science, Earth observation and computational modelling. The goal is to train researchers who can lead the digital transformation of science in their own field.

Project: Integration of remote sensing and epidemiological models for the operational surveillance and risk assessment of emerging plant diseases in a climate change context
Programme: CSIC MOMENTUM Programme for attracting and retaining digital talent · Ref. MMT24-PTI-SOLXYL-01
Framework: CSIC Interdisciplinary Thematic Platform PTI SOL-XYL – Innovative approaches for research and solutions to diseases caused by Xylella fastidiosa in cultivated plants (coordinator: Dr. Blanca B. Landa)
Role: MOMENTUM Postdoctoral Researcher
Host institution: Institute for Sustainable Agriculture (IAS-CSIC), Córdoba, Spain

title: MOMENTUM: Remote sensing and epidemiological modelling for the surveillance of emerging plant diseases
text:
Overview
The spread of emerging plant diseases, intensified by climate change and globalisation, threatens crop production and food supply chains. This project proposes a “digital plant pathology” approach for Xylella fastidiosa, ranked as the top priority plant pest in the European Union.
The new era of open hyperspectral satellite data and artificial intelligence is transforming plant epidemiology. Hyperspectral satellites combine the operational coverage that airborne sensors lack with a continuous spectrum that multispectral satellites cannot provide, allowing a more accurate quantification of the physiological and biochemical traits of plants and of their response to pathogens. By feeding these observations into epidemiological and species distribution models, the project overcomes the lack of data that limits current predictions, and turns them into risk assessments that are useful for agricultural and governmental decision-makers.
The work focuses on crops affected by X. fastidiosa in Spain, mainly almond and grapevine.

title: MOMENTUM: Remote sensing and epidemiological modelling for the surveillance of emerging plant diseases
text:
Objectives

Evaluate the use of hyperspectral and multispectral satellite imagery for the detection and monitoring of diseases caused by X. fastidiosa in cultivated plants at regional scale.

1.1. Analyse the accuracy and contribution of spectral traits of cultivated plants and surrounding wild vegetation retrieved through Radiative Transfer Models (RTMs), using high-spatial-resolution (<1 m) hyperspectral and thermal data and field data as reference, to detect early, intermediate and severe levels of symptom severity.
1.2. Develop generalisable machine learning (ML) algorithms based on satellite imagery for the operational monitoring of diseases caused by X. fastidiosa.

Integrate hyperspectral and multispectral satellite imagery into epidemiological models to improve their parameterisation and optimise the surveillance and control of diseases caused by X. fastidiosa.

2.1. Quantitatively assess epidemiological parameters essential for risk assessment.
2.2. Develop optimised statistical strategies to inform surveillance and control programmes for diseases caused by X. fastidiosa.

Improve the risk assessment of emerging diseases in the context of climate change by integrating satellite data, species distribution models and epidemiological disease spread models.

3.1. Identify the underlying biotic and abiotic factors that promote the establishment and spread of diseases caused by X. fastidiosa in agricultural ecosystems.
3.2. Investigate the implications of climate change and land use for the risk of establishment and spread of diseases caused by X. fastidiosa.

title: MOMENTUM: Remote sensing and epidemiological modelling for the surveillance of emerging plant diseases
text:
Approach
We propose a synergistic approach that combines the strengths of hyperspectral and multispectral satellite remote sensing for the detection and monitoring of emerging plant diseases. The high spectral resolution of hyperspectral satellite data will enable the accurate quantification of plant functional traits that are sensitive to the progression of biotic stress, including chlorophyll fluorescence, while the high spatial resolution of multispectral satellite data will allow the identification of the components of the scene, facilitating the parameterisation of radiative transfer models. These functional traits, together with spectral vegetation indices, will be estimated with radiative transfer models and integrated into supervised machine learning classification models, using disease incidence and symptom severity data collected in field campaigns, as well as high-spatial-resolution hyperspectral and thermal imagery, as benchmark.
The high temporal coverage of hyperspectral and multispectral satellite data will improve the assessment of the spatio-temporal dynamics of pathogen infections, capturing the seasonal transmission by insect vectors. By integrating these data into epidemiological models, more accurate models can be built to predict the spread of insect-transmitted diseases such as X. fastidiosa. We will design a stochastic, spatially explicit compartmental model that incorporates the seasonal movements of the vectors and the different epidemiological states of the plants over time, using time series of disease indicators derived from hyperspectral and multispectral satellite data. We will apply Bayesian inference to fit the model parameters using both visual field inspection data and satellite data, in order to compare both estimates. This parameterised model will include simulation modules to evaluate the effectiveness of different surveillance and control strategies.
To improve the risk assessment of emerging diseases, species distribution models will be adapted to incorporate pathogen dispersal through the previously parameterised epidemiological model, thus capturing the dynamic interaction between vector, host, pathogen and environment. Publicly available occurrence data of the pathogen and its vectors will be used, and hyperspectral and multispectral satellite data will be employed to map susceptible hosts and the environmental factors that favour disease development. We will integrate these data into species distribution models to generate current disease risk maps and to identify the most relevant abiotic and biotic factors for disease establishment. These factors will then be obtained from climate simulations of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), or its updates, to explore the implications of future climate change and land use. By incorporating pathogen dispersal, we will estimate the risk of persistence and subsequent epidemic development when the pathogen is randomly introduced into pathogen-free areas, enabling the design of proactive surveillance protocols.

title: MOMENTUM: Remote sensing and epidemiological modelling for the surveillance of emerging plant diseases
text:
Expected impact
The new era of open satellite data, artificial intelligence and computational biology is revolutionising plant epidemiology, driving a new paradigm in the understanding, surveillance and control of emerging plant diseases. This project stands at the forefront of this change, aiming to achieve accurate detection, real-time monitoring and robust assessment of the risk of disease establishment and spread in a context of climate change. This synergy will make it possible to design more precise and efficient surveillance and control strategies, preventing and mitigating the adverse impacts of emerging diseases such as X. fastidiosa on crops.
In addition, this research will advance the field of Earth observation by aligning with the objectives of the European Space Agency (ESA) to improve operational applications related to food security and sustainable agriculture, and to support data-driven plant health policy-making. The project also fits within the Horizon Europe 2021–2024 strategic plan. By taking advantage of advances in digital and data technologies, together with Earth observation applications for monitoring, modelling and forecasting, it will help to increase the resilience and sustainability of agricultural systems and improve their capacity to respond to plant pathogens, especially in the context of the potential aggravating effects of climate.

title: Integrating spread modelling and remote sensing to optimise early detection surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union
text:
Overview

Background
Xylella fastidiosa is considered one of the most dangerous plant pathogenic bacteria in the world. First detected in Europe in 2013 in olive trees in Apulia (southern Italy), where it causes Olive Quick Decline Syndrome, it has since been found in France, Spain and other countries, and it can infect more than 550 host species. Its spread threatens the large Mediterranean areas planted with olive, almond, citrus and grapevine, and the EU has made early detection a cornerstone of its plant health regulation.
Epidemiological models are increasingly used to simulate how epidemics spread across landscapes and to design surveillance and control strategies that maximise the chances of eradication while minimising costs. Remote sensing, in turn, can monitor very large areas quickly and, with high-resolution hyperspectral and thermal sensors, detect the physiological changes caused by vascular pathogens.


Knowledge gaps

Long asymptomatic period. Olive trees infected by X. fastidiosa can take around 10 months or more to show symptoms, while surveillance in Europe relies mainly on visual inspection. Infected but asymptomatic trees keep spreading the pathogen undetected.
Costly and biased field surveillance. Field surveys are labour-intensive and expensive, so they are limited to small areas and are often spatially biased, giving a distorted picture of the real state of the epidemic.
Poorly parameterised models. Spread models depend on parameters estimated from scarce and imperfect inspection data, which limits their ability to predict emerging epidemics accurately.
Remote sensing and spread models were disconnected. It was unclear what remote sensing could reveal about epidemic dynamics, and how it could be combined with spread models to estimate disease distribution and to target surveillance.


Project aim: to optimise the surveillance and early detection of Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union by integrating epidemic spread models with airborne hyperspectral and thermal remote sensing, from the detection of pre-visual infections to the design of surveillance and control strategies.

title: Integrating spread modelling and remote sensing to optimise early detection surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union
text:
Study areas

Apulia, Italy: X. fastidiosa subsp. pauca in olive orchards, with airborne campaigns in 2016 and 2017 and field inspections of about 3,300 trees per year in 15 plots.
Alicante, Spain: X. fastidiosa subsp. multiplex in almond orchards, with an airborne campaign in 2018 and field inspections of 1,453 trees in 20 plots, 328 of them tested by qPCR.

Airborne campaigns were carried out by the European Commission Joint Research Centre and IAS-CSIC within the H2020 projects XF-ACTORS and POnTE.

title: Integrating spread modelling and remote sensing to optimise early detection surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union
text:
Key results at a glance


80.9% accuracy detecting X. fastidiosa in olive from plant traits


61% of asymptomatic trees flagged by remote sensing showed symptoms within 4 months (vs 39%)


35% → 50% qPCR-confirmed infections detected in almond after coupling the spread model

title: Integrating spread modelling and remote sensing to optimise early detection surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union
text:
Approach: three work packages


 1 · Remote sensing detection
Automatic methods for the early detection of X. fastidiosa at landscape scale from airborne hyperspectral and thermal imagery:

Plant functional traits retrieved by radiative transfer model inversion (pigments, structure, nitrogen-related indices), chlorophyll fluorescence and canopy temperature.
Machine learning classifiers (support vector machines, neural networks, linear discriminant analysis) trained on field inspections.
Multi-temporal revisits of trees over two years, supported by qPCR, to test pre-visual detection.



 2 · Estimating disease distribution
A stochastic optimisation model that estimates the spatial distribution of X. fastidiosa from a sample by combining:

Landscape connectivity of the host population (graph and circuit theory) and distance-dependent dispersal.
Remote sensing infection probabilities for each tree.

Developed and validated in Italy and then transferred to the almond orchards of Alicante.


 3 · Spatio-temporal spread modelling
A stochastic, spatially explicit spread model for X. fastidiosa in Italy, parameterised with two data sources, field inspections and remote sensing, to compare:

The epidemiological parameters estimated from each source.
The effectiveness of different surveillance and control scenarios, such as revisit intervals, detection probability and host removal radius.

title: Integrating spread modelling and remote sensing to optimise early detection surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union
text:
Main findings


 Pre-visual detection

Plant traits related to pigments and structure, together with chlorophyll fluorescence and temperature, detected infected olive trees with 80.9% accuracy (κ = 0.61), against 65.4% using only the RGB–NIR indices typical of satellite sensors.
Trees flagged by remote sensing but still asymptomatic in the field were significantly more likely to develop symptoms in the following months, confirming that infection can be detected before visible symptoms appear.



 Almond orchards in Alicante

Adding nitrogen-related indices from the SWIR region to fluorescence and temperature gave the best detection of X. fastidiosa in almond (74.0% accuracy, κ = 0.48).
Accuracy dropped in orchards with low disease incidence, precisely where early detection matters most.



 Remote sensing + spread models

Combining remote sensing with landscape connectivity and dispersal gave more realistic estimates of disease distribution in low-incidence orchards than remote sensing alone.
Coupling the spread model with remote sensing increased the detection of qPCR-confirmed infections in almond from 35% to 50%.

title: Integrating spread modelling and remote sensing to optimise early detection surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa in the European Union
text:
Take-home message
High-resolution hyperspectral and thermal remote sensing can detect Xylella fastidiosa infections before symptoms are visible, and combining it with epidemic spread models improves estimates of where the disease is, especially at the early stages of an outbreak when control is still possible. This work opened a line of research that I continue today in the MOMENTUM project, moving these approaches to satellite data and operational surveillance.

title: Soilborne plant pathogen dispersal and assessment: a remote sensing-based global surveillance system for Fusarium wilt
text:
Overview

Background
Plant diseases destroy around 15% of the food grown worldwide, with annual losses of roughly US$220 billion, and fungi cause about 80% of them, many of the most aggressive being soilborne. Fusarium oxysporum, the causal agent of Fusarium wilt, ranks among the ten most damaging fungal plant pathogens: it is present on all six crop-producing continents, infects more than 100 host species, causes yield losses of 10–60% and produces resistant spores that can survive in the soil for decades. New virulent strains able to overcome host resistance, such as Tropical Race 4 in banana, and a warmer climate that expands its suitable range make it a growing threat to food security.
At the same time, wind erosion of dry agricultural land is an important source of atmospheric dust, and soil microbes travel attached to dust particles. Spores and DNA of F. oxysporum have been found in North African and Asian dust samples, raising the possibility that soilborne pathogens can spread across continents through the atmosphere.


Knowledge gaps

No global surveillance system for crop diseases. International efforts to monitor plant disease outbreaks are limited by scarce resources and poor information exchange, and remote sensing has rarely been considered as part of the solution: the disciplines of plant pathology and Earth observation remain largely disconnected.
Coarse and incomplete risk assessments. Global assessments of Fusarium wilt risk rely on sparse surveillance records and coarse climate data, and ignore the distribution and activity of susceptible crops and other environmental drivers that satellites can now measure.
Unknown role of airborne dispersal. Long-distance dispersal of foliar pathogens is well studied, but whether soilborne pathogens travel with global dust currents has never been demonstrated, and management recommendations for soilborne diseases do not consider airborne spread at any scale.
Unknown genetic basis of dispersal. Little is known about which plant pathogens actually travel with dust, or about the spore traits that allow them to survive atmospheric transport.


Project aim: to bridge plant pathology and Earth observation by combining satellite remote sensing, aerosol transport modelling and comparative genomics, and to lay the foundations of a remote sensing-based global surveillance system that maps the risk of Fusarium wilt and the atmospheric dispersal of F. oxysporum under current and future climate.

title: Soilborne plant pathogen dispersal and assessment: a remote sensing-based global surveillance system for Fusarium wilt
text:
Objectives

Susceptibility assessment: identify agricultural regions that are both suitable for Fusarium wilt and arid enough to act as dust sources, using satellite-derived environmental, vegetation and cropland data.
Atmospheric transport modelling: evaluate the risk of global pathogen movement by simulating the entrainment, transport and deposition of spores carried by aerosolised agricultural soil.
Comparative genomics: compare F. oxysporum genomes from isolates spanning many host species to identify genetic traits that influence spore dispersal, atmospheric survival and pathogenicity.
Integration and prediction: combine these components into a remote sensing-based risk assessment of the global incidence of F. oxysporum under different climate change scenarios.

title: Soilborne plant pathogen dispersal and assessment: a remote sensing-based global surveillance system for Fusarium wilt
text:
Approach: three research pillars
The project combined three disciplines that rarely work together, each answering a different part of the question.


 1 · Remote sensing risk assessment
Fusarium wilt risk was mapped within the plant disease triangle framework, where disease results from a virulent pathogen infecting a susceptible host in a conducive environment:

Pathogen: a public global web map with more than 4,500 F. oxysporum records from the peer-reviewed literature.
Host: Landsat cropland fraction, MODIS land cover dynamics and solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) as a proxy for crop activity.
Environment: long-term satellite products of land surface and air temperature, precipitation, soil moisture and evapotranspiration.

These layers fed an ensemble of species distribution algorithms at 1 km resolution, projected to 2100 under three CMIP6 climate scenarios.


 2 · Aerosol transport modelling
The Earth system model CESM2-CAM6 was adapted, through the MIMI dust framework, to include agricultural dust emissions and the concentration of F. oxysporum spores in soil estimated from the web map.
Spore viability during transport was simulated with an exponential decay function driven by UV exposure. The model was tested with the “Godzilla” dust storm of June 2020, which carried Saharan dust to the south-eastern United States.


 3 · Comparative genomics
Dust samples were collected from air filters before, during and after a major dust event at two deposition sites, Cayenne (French Guiana) and Barbados, and cultured to identify the fungi travelling with dust.
Genomic analyses were used to identify plant pathogens in the dust and the spore traits that may affect dispersal and atmospheric survival, combined with HYSPLIT back-trajectories of the air masses.

title: Soilborne plant pathogen dispersal and assessment: a remote sensing-based global surveillance system for Fusarium wilt
text:
Main findings


 Fusarium wilt risk

About 20.7% of global land and 70.8% of cropland are currently suitable for Fusarium wilt.
Suitability is driven by temperature and soil moisture, and shaped by cropland extent and host activity (SIF).
Risk expands by 2100 in all climate scenarios, mainly through warming at mid- to high northern latitudes and cropland expansion and hydrological change in northern Sub-Saharan Africa, while several Southern Hemisphere regions show net losses.



 Long-distance spore transport

During the Godzilla storm, about 13,000 of 4 trillion spores from North Africa reached the Americas still viable, with Mexico and the Caribbean as the areas at highest risk of deposition on cropland.
Globally, transport is dominated by Eurasia–Africa interactions, and Sub-Saharan Africa is the main hub, the source of 53% of all viable spore deposition.



 Pathogens in dust

Dust carried diverse fungal communities with potential plant and human pathogens, such as Colletotrichum and Cladosporium, plus many rare taxa.
F. oxysporum spores were abundant in Cayenne after the dust storm, supporting the modelling evidence of long-distance transport.

title: Soilborne plant pathogen dispersal and assessment: a remote sensing-based global surveillance system for Fusarium wilt
text:
Take-home message
Pathosystem distribution modelling turns remote sensing data streams into actionable risk assessments. Fusarium wilt risk will expand regardless of the climate change scenario, and both models and genomic data show that soilborne pathogens can travel long distances with dust. The project lays the foundation for using the new generation of hyperspectral satellites, together with other remote sensing tools, in a global surveillance system for crop diseases, a line of work I continue in the MOMENTUM project.

title: IAS-CSIC Seminar: Remote sensing and epidemiological models for plant disease surveillance
text:
On 28 March 2025 I gave a talk in the IAS-CSIC Seminar Series at the Institute for Sustainable Agriculture in Córdoba: “Integración de teledetección y modelos epidemiológicos para la vigilancia operativa y la evaluación del riesgo de enfermedades en plantas en el contexto del cambio climático” (Integrating remote sensing and epidemiological models for the operational surveillance and risk assessment of plant diseases in the context of climate change).
In the seminar I explained how satellite data can be combined with epidemiological and species distribution models to monitor plant diseases and assess their risk under climate change, the research line of my MOMENTUM project.
The seminar was streamed live and the recording is available on the IAS-CSIC YouTube channel (the talk is in Spanish):
